outcome.answer:
Internal representations of language models seem to correlate with human effort in understanding sentences in a layered way: early layers better track human processing for naturalistic reading, while later layers better estimate the extra cognitive effort in syntactically challenging or ambiguous sentences, though they still underestimate the human data [1]. More generally, papers here find that LM features linked to surprisal, hidden-layer structure, and other internal measures predict reading difficulty and reading times, with some measures capturing complementary aspects of processing load [1, 5, 9].

The same general pattern appears in brain and representation studies: sparse or hidden LM features align nontrivially with language brain responses [2, 3, 6], and internal representations can encode grammaticality beyond raw string probability [7, 8].
